source.title: Unsolved and Unsolvable Problems in Geometry

accepted.question_text: For a given integer n, place n points on the unit sphere so that the minimum distance between any two points is as large as possible. Equivalently, determine the smallest sphere radius r on which n points can be placed with every pair at distance at least 1.

evidence.quote: (1) We are given a spherical planet and 10 (n, in general) mutually hostile dictators. How can the capital cities of these gentlemen be distributed on the sphere so that the minimum distance between any two of them is as great as possible ? This problem is equivalent to the following :—What is the smallest radius r of a sphere on which 10 (n, in general) points can be placed at a minimum distance of 1 unit apart?

accepted.question_text: For a given integer n, place n points on a sphere so that every point of the sphere is as close as possible to its nearest chosen point. Equivalently, determine the smallest radius of n congruent spherical caps needed to cover the unit sphere.

evidence.quote: (2) On any spherical planet n(n = 9, 10, 11, ...) fuel depots may be placed so that the distance of any point on the surface from the nearest depot is as small as possible.
Problem (2a): The unit sphere must be completely covered by n spherical caps of smallest possible radius.

accepted.question_text: Determine how congruent spheres should be packed in three-dimensional Euclidean space so that the packing density is as large as possible.

evidence.quote: (3) How should one pack a set of congruent spheres (in three- dimensional space) so that the density of packing is as great as possible ?

accepted.question_text: Among all convex plane sets that can cover every plane point set of diameter 1, determine the exact minimum possible area and characterize all minimizing tiles. The source notes that a minimal convex tile exists, but the practical determination of one or more minimal tiles remains open.

evidence.quote: (4a) Let to be the lower bound of the surface area t(7) of all convex tiles. (a) The value of to is to be determined. (b) Jt is to be ascertained whether there exists a tile of F with area equal to To. (c) If there exist tiles with minimal area, are all tiles F with surface measure Tt, of the form to be determined later ?
The problem of the practical determination of one or more minimal tiles is stil] open.

accepted.question_text: Determine the smallest possible density of a rigid packing of congruent circles in the plane, where rigidity means that every circle is touched by at least three other circles in such a way that displacement without overlap is impossible.

evidence.quote: A packing of non-overlapping circles in the plane f is said to be rigid if every circle is touched by at least three other circles so that the points of contact on any of the circles are less than a semi-circle apart.
Probably this is the smallest possible value for the density of a rigid packing of circles.

accepted.question_text: For each integer k greater than 1, determine the extremal density d_k of k-fold packings of congruent circles in the plane and the extremal density D_k of k-fold coverings of the plane by congruent circles, where every point belongs to at most k circles in a k-fold packing and to at least k circles in a k-fold covering.

evidence.quote: If every point of the plane is covered by at most k (congruent) circles, then we speak of a k-fold packing of circles. If every point belongs to at least k circles then there is a k-fold covering of the plane.
There still remains the open question :— How large are the numbers d, = lim 6,, D, = lim A, fork>\1?

accepted.question_text: In extremal coverings of the unit sphere by congruent spherical caps, must an intersection point where four covering arcs meet (an I-point of order 4) always be absent from the extremal covering graph?

evidence.quote: i, is not noted since an J-point of order 4 did not occur in any of the extremal graphs found so far. However, at present, it has not been proved that this must always be the case.

accepted.question_text: Determine the smallest possible density of a rigid packing of congruent spheres in three-dimensional space.

evidence.quote: It is conjectured that this is the smallest value for the density of a rigid packing of spheres [II 3]. This has not yet been proved true.

accepted.question_text: Suppose a family of disks in the plane has the property that every two disks intersect, but the radii of the disks are allowed to vary. Determine whether four points always suffice so that every disk in the family contains at least one of those points.

evidence.quote: One can generalise the problem considered here and ask by how many points can a set 9’ of disks be fixed if each two disks of this set have an (interior) point in common but the radii may be different. One knows that 5 points suffice and L. Fryes TOTH conjectures that one can also manage with 4 points.

accepted.question_text: Find a three-dimensional covering body of smallest volume that contains every point set in Euclidean 3-space whose diameter is 1.

evidence.quote: This result suggests the problem of finding a covering body (D-body) of smallest volume for a cluster of points of diameter 1 of 23.

accepted.question_text: Determine a sufficient criterion for when two polyhedra of equal volume are equivalent by dissection. In particular, decide whether Dehn's necessary condition together with equality of volume is already sufficient, equivalently whether polyhedra whose remaining obstruction has all dihedral angles equal to multiples of pi/4 must be dissection-equivalent to a cube.

evidence.quote: The problem of finding sufficient conditions for equivalence by dissection is not completely solved.
If one could manage to show also that such poly- hedra are equivalent to a cube, one would have proved that the necessary condition (1) (together with equality of the volume) is also sufficient.

accepted.question_text: Determine the smallest number n of pairwise incongruent squares into which a square can be dissected so that the dissection is perfect, meaning that no two constituent squares are congruent.

evidence.quote: (6) Which is the smallest number n (n', n") of squares used (6a) in a perfect (simple, simple and perfect) decomposition of (6b) a square?

accepted.question_text: Determine the smallest number n'' of squares in a dissection of a square that is both simple, meaning it cannot be split into smaller rectangular groups, and perfect, meaning no two constituent squares are congruent.

evidence.quote: (6) Which is the smallest number n (n', n") of squares used (6a) in a perfect (simple, simple and perfect) decomposition of (6b) a square?
The number 7 (problem (6)) is still unknown and so isn".

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a countably infinite subset of the Euclidean plane that is dense in the whole plane and has the property that the distance between every two of its points is a rational number?

evidence.quote: A problem which is still unsolved [VIII 5] and which should be mentioned in this connection is the following :— (7b) Is there a denumerable, infinite set which is everywhere dense in the whole plane and for which every two points have a rational distance apart ?

accepted.question_text: Can a circular disk and a square of the same area be partitioned into finitely many pairwise congruent subsets if the pieces are allowed to be arbitrary sets rather than polygons?

evidence.quote: (10) The set-theoretical squaring problem:—The circular disk @ (x*+y?<1) and the square Ff of equal area (OSxS.J7; O<ys./z) may be sub-divided into a finite number n of subsets @, and &, in such a way that the subsets with the same subscript are congruent
Therefore it makes sense to pose the squaring problem in the geometry of sets (problem (10), p. 4). It is still unsolved.
